headline: Senators Demand Crackdown on Wildfire Betting Markets Amid Arson Fears
deck: Lawmakers from five states urge federal regulators to halt platforms allowing wagers on catastrophic blazes, citing dangerous incentives and ethical dilemmas surrounding disaster profiteering.
body: US senators from five states have urged the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to halt prediction markets that allow individuals to bet on wildfire outcomes, citing heightened risks of arson and the unethical profiting from disaster.

The lawmakers' letter comes as active wildfires continue to burn across the Pacific Northwest, bringing tangible devastation. In Spokane, Washington, several hundred buildings have already been destroyed, forcing approximately one-quarter of the city’s population to evacuate.

The immediate danger of such markets became stark recently when the Spokane County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrest of an arson suspect. This individual is believed to have started one of the blazes currently threatening Spokane, underscoring the very risks cited by senators.

Polymarket, a prominent prediction market platform, previously hosted contracts in January 2025 that allowed users to wager on wildfire events in Los Angeles. The platform claims it does not currently have any active markets on wildfires and has not for some time.
Wildfire experts expressed outrage at the very concept of these markets. They argue that the mere existence of platforms allowing trading on such disasters is appalling.

"Offering bets on destructive wildfires threatens to minimize communities’ suffering, all so the rich and powerful can profit," the senators stated in their letter to the CFTC. This sentiment highlights the profound ethical objections underpinning their demand for regulatory intervention.

Polymarket, however, asserts that it does not profit from market outcomes and that users primarily come to the platform for information. The company argues that restricting these markets could hinder access to valuable data.

"While we are not blind to the risks, removing these markets does not prevent a tragedy but makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most," a Polymarket representative stated. This position suggests a belief in the informational utility of such markets, even in sensitive areas.

Other platforms in the prediction market space take a different approach. Kalshi, for example, explicitly prohibits wildfire markets, citing the potential for "perverse incentives" that could encourage destructive behavior.

The CFTC has yet to respond to the senators' request for comment, leaving the regulatory future of these controversial markets uncertain. This ongoing debate pits the speculative potential of prediction platforms against the dire public safety concerns raised by lawmakers and disaster experts.
